Miasma/Hades auto-exec editor & AI-tool config files dropped in project tree AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the StepSecurity-named 'Suspicious Files' that the Miasma/Hades worm plants into a repository so code runs the moment a developer opens the folder or starts an AI coding session — .claude/setup.mjs, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, .vscode/tasks.json (runOn:folderOpen), .vscode/setup.mjs, .github/setup.js. Also matches the campaign's known payload SHA256s. These artifacts never appear in package.json or a lockfile diff, so SCA/registry gateways miss them. Rationale: Uses the exact file/path matrix StepSecurity published (.claude/setup.mjs, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, .vscode/tasks.json, .vscode/setup.mjs, .github/setup.js) plus the campaign's five payload SHA256s, cross-checked against Socket.dev and JFrog write-ups of the same Miasma/Hades wave. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately scaffolds a .vscode/tasks.json build task or .claude/settings.json team config and commits it
  • Project templates / cookiecutters that ship a .github or .vscode folder
  • A teammate cloning a known-good internal repo that intentionally uses .cursor/rules
  • VS Code or Cursor itself writing settings.json during normal use
  • Dotfile-manager tools syncing editor configs across machines
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("settings.json","tasks.json") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","cursor.exe","devenv.exe","git.exe") and FolderPath !has "node_modules")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the flagged file and read it — legit tasks.json/settings.json contain JSON config; malicious variants contain a setup.mjs/setup.js loader, an obfuscated one-liner, or a 'runOn: folderOpen' task that shells out (node, curl, bun). Check git blame / commit author for an unexpected or recently re-compromised contributor. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the developer host, revoke that user's npm and PyPI publish tokens (~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc) and any GitHub PAT, and quarantine the repo from CI. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC 'Hades Bun runtime' and 'mass publish' detections on the same host; search the org's other repos for the same file paths/hashes; review what packages the leaked tokens could publish.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Phantom Gyp: malicious binding.gyp executing during npm install AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' technique — a ~157-byte binding.gyp dropped into a package so node-gyp executes attacker code during the native build step, bypassing preinstall/postinstall script controls. Matches binding.gyp written by npm/node tooling that is abnormally small or matches a known campaign hash. Rationale: Anchors on the article's concrete 'Phantom Gyp' detail — a 157-byte binding.gyp that fires during the native build — plus the campaign SHA256 set; Snyk independently documents the same self-propagating binding.gyp npm worm. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate native npm module ships a genuinely tiny binding.gyp stub
  • Developer hand-authoring a minimal binding.gyp while prototyping a node addon
  • node-gyp regenerating binding.gyp under node_modules during a clean install of a trusted dependency
  • Monorepo build tooling templating placeholder gyp files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "node_modules" and FileSize between (100 .. 511) and SHA256 !in ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe","e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d","c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c","7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655","b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: cat the binding.gyp — a benign one declares 'targets'/'sources'; the Phantom Gyp variant abuses a gyp 'action'/'rule' to invoke node/curl/bun or contains an inline command. Identify the owning package and whether it was just installed/updated. 2) CONTAIN: Kill any node-gyp/node child it spawned, isolate the host, and revoke npm/PyPI tokens reachable from it. 3) HUNT: Correlate with UC 'Hades Bun runtime' and 'mass publish' on the same host within the install window; check which package version pulled it in and pull that version from your registry/cache.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileSize < 512    // Phantom Gyp payload is ~157 bytes; real native-module configs are far larger
    or SHA256 in ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe","e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d","c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c","7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655","b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileSize < 512
    or TargetFileSHA256 in ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe","e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d","c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c","7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655","b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades on-import payload: Python process spawning Bun JavaScript runtime AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Hades PyPI execution chain — a poisoned package's import/startup hook downloads a standalone, signed Bun runtime and runs an obfuscated JavaScript stealer. A python.exe/pip process spawning bun is highly abnormal in an enterprise and is the cleanest behavioural signal for the memory-resident stealer (no malware binary to fingerprint). Rationale: Built on the article's core Hades behaviour — import-time download and execution of a standalone Bun runtime — corroborated by The Hacker News and Socket.dev (Bun stealer fetched at Python startup); python-spawns-bun is rare enough to alert. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave • https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/hades-campaign-pypi-shai-hulud
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who legitimately uses Bun and invokes it from a Python build/orchestration script
  • Polyglot monorepo tooling where a Python task runner shells out to bun for a JS sub-build
  • CI agent images that pre-warm both Python and Bun toolchains
  • A data-science notebook subprocess launching bun for a frontend asset step
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\build\\","frontend","vite","esbuild") and DeviceName has_any ("build","ci","runner"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the bun command line and the parent python command line — capture which package's __init__.py/.pth triggered it and what URL the bun payload was fetched from. Pull the bun child's network connections. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the bun process, and immediately rotate every credential reachable from that developer (npm/PyPI tokens, cloud keys, GitHub PAT) since the payload reads secrets from process memory. 3) HUNT: Search org-wide for python-spawns-bun and for the Hades *-setup.pth artifact; identify the offending PyPI package + version and block it in your index/proxy.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun.exe" or FileName =~ "bun" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Bun"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3","pythonw.exe","pip.exe","pip3")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="bun.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bun") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="bun.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bun") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Hades PyPI startup hook: malicious -setup.pth dropped in site-packages AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Hades persistence/trigger artifact independent vendors confirmed — a '*-setup.pth' file planted in Python site-packages/dist-packages that executes at interpreter startup to fetch the Bun runtime. .pth files run any line beginning with 'import', so a campaign-named setup.pth is an on-startup code-execution hook that SCA scanners never inspect. Rationale: Adds the '*-setup.pth' startup-hook artifact that Socket.dev/JFrog/The Hacker News independently tied to the Hades wave (the article only names __init__.py); .pth-in-site-packages with a campaign naming convention is a high-fidelity, low-FP file signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave • https://thecybersecguru.com/news/hades-pypi-malware-miasma-supply-chain-attack/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate package whose distribution genuinely ships a '<name>-setup.pth' (rare but possible for editable installs)
  • setuptools/pip writing __editable__.*.pth or distutils-precedence.pth during normal installs
  • Virtualenv creation copying a base-environment .pth into a new site-packages
  • In-house package using a .pth for namespace path configuration
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("distutils-precedence.pth","__editable__.pth") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe") and FileName startswith "__editable__")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the .pth file — a benign one contains only directory paths; the Hades variant has an 'import ...' one-liner that decodes/execs and reaches out for Bun. Note the package name embedded in the filename. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, delete/quarantine the .pth, and rotate npm/PyPI/cloud tokens for that developer. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC 'python spawns Bun' on the same host around startup; query DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory / pip freeze across the fleet for the offending package and block the version at your PyPI proxy.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where FolderPath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades PyPI - Malicious setup.pth Startup Hook in site-packages
id: c5f3e4d6-7d80-49ca-be23-4f5a6b7c8d9e
description: Detects creation of a '*-setup.pth' file in Python site-packages/dist-packages, the Hades worm's interpreter-startup code-execution hook that fetches the Bun runtime.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
  - https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1546
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    FileName|endswith: '-setup.pth'
    FolderPath|contains:
      - 'site-packages'
      - 'dist-packages'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*-setup.pth OR *-setup.PTH OR *-SETUP.PTH) @TargetFilename:(*site-packages* OR *dist-packages*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/-setup\.pth$/i
| regex("(site-packages|dist-packages)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*-setup.pth" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*dist-packages*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*-setup.pth" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*dist-packages*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Worm propagation: burst of npm/PyPI publishes from a developer machine AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the self-replication stage — once Miasma/Hades steals npm/PyPI publishing tokens it republishes infected versions of every package the token can publish. A developer endpoint emitting many 'npm publish' or 'twine upload' invocations in a tight window is automated mass-republish behaviour, not human activity. Thresholded so a normal one-off release won't fire. Rationale: Targets the worm's defining self-replication behaviour described in the article (steal publish tokens, republish every package the token allows) as a publish-burst threshold; cross-checked against JFrog/Socket reporting that the same actor mass-republished across npm and PyPI. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/ • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave • https://phoenix.security/miasma-azure-hades-pypi-supply-chain-worm-2026/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A release engineer running a monorepo/Lerna/changesets publish that pushes many packages at once
  • CI release pipeline executing on a developer's machine instead of a build agent
  • Bulk version bump + publish during a coordinated multi-package release
  • Internal tooling that publishes a fleet of private scoped packages on each merge
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("build","ci","runner","release") or AccountName in~ ("svc-release","build-agent"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Review the SampleCmds — confirm whether this was an intended coordinated release (check change tickets / release calendar) and which registry/scope was targeted; legitimate bulk releases come from a known release owner on a known host. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, immediately revoke the npm/PyPI publish tokens used, force-unpublish/yank the just-published versions, and isolate the host. 3) HUNT: Pull this host's UC 'python spawns Bun' / 'suspicious config files' hits to find the infection vector; enumerate every package the leaked token can publish and audit those for tampered versions in the last 24h.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "publish" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","npm-cli.js","twine")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize PublishCount = count(), SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where PublishCount >= 5    // 5+ publishes in 10 min = automated mass republish; a human dev publishes 1-2
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "publish" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","npm-cli.js","twine")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize PublishCount = count(), SampleCmds = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where PublishCount >= 5    // 5+ publishes in 10 min = automated mass republish; a human dev publishes 1-2
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*publish* (@CommandLine:*npm* OR @CommandLine:*twine*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("publish", field=CommandLine)
| (regex("npm", field=CommandLine) OR regex("twine", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count(as=PublishCount))
| PublishCount >= 5
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process="*twine*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 5
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process="*twine*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 5
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:

detection:

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XXE parameter-entity OOB exfil: rare/long-label DNS callback from FHIR Java host — CVE-2026-55471
Blind XXE / SSRF: FHIR Java process fetches external DTD or XSLT stylesheet — CVE-2026-55471 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the exploitation side-effect of the unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory: with ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/STYLESHEET unset, the parser resolves external DTDs and stylesheets, so the FHIR/Java server makes an outbound request to an attacker URL ending in .dtd/.xsl/.xslt. Backend FHIR servers rarely fetch remote stylesheets, making this high-signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's root cause — saxonTransform resolving external DTD/stylesheet because ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/STYLESHEET are unset — expressed as a java-process / proxy egress to a .dtd/.xsl/.xslt URL, with public-DTD hosts (w3.org/oasis) filtered to cut benign XSLT toolchains. Falcon/Datadog fall back to java→public-IP since FDR/Sysmon network events carry no URL path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/ca.uhn.hapi.fhir/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/CVE-2026-55471/ • https://saxonica.plan.io/issues/4729
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java applications legitimately fetching remote XSLT stylesheets for report rendering
  • Document/IG publishing pipelines resolving public DTDs (already filtered for w3.org/oasis/docbook)
  • Internal CI servers running XSLT transforms against an internal artifact repo over HTTP
  • RemoteUrl unpopulated by Defender when web content filtering is off, causing under-detection rather than FP
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("w3.org","oasis-open.org","docbook.org","xml.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the destination host/URL and whether it is attacker-controlled (new domain, raw IP, recently registered); confirm the initiating process is the FHIR/Java service and correlate to a preceding inbound XML POST (UC 1). 2) Contain: block the destination at egress proxy/firewall and isolate the FHIR host if the fetched resource looks like an attacker DTD; capture the JVM's outbound connection list. 3) Hunt: check DeviceFileEvents on that host for java.exe reads of sensitive paths (file:// general-entity disclosure) and run the DNS-callback UC for parameter-entity OOB exfil.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl has_any (".dtd",".xsl",".xslt")
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("w3.org","oasis-open.org","docbook.org"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (".dtd",".xsl",".xslt")
| where not(Url has_any ("w3.org","oasis-open.org","docbook.org"))
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XXE parameter-entity OOB exfil: rare/long-label DNS callback from FHIR Java host — CVE-2026-55471 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the out-of-band exfiltration channel of the blind XXE: a parameter-entity (<!ENTITY % p SYSTEM ...>) smuggles local file contents into a DNS subdomain label, producing a first-seen external domain or an abnormally long leftmost DNS label sourced from the FHIR/Java process. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit parameter-entity OOB primitive (<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://...">) by hunting the DNS side-channel from the java process: first-seen external domain (Defender) or 30+ char leftmost label (Sentinel/Falcon/Splunk DNS-exfil heuristic). Datadog left empty — Sysmon DNS (EID 22) is not in the shipped sysmon event set. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud/CDN telemetry domains that use long hashed leftmost labels (telemetry, antivirus reputation lookups)
  • Legitimate Java apps doing service discovery against long auto-generated hostnames
  • First-seen anti-join firing on a newly onboarded but benign integration endpoint
  • DNS over a corporate resolver that rewrites/long-encodes names
Suppression filter
| where not(DnsQuery has_any ("akamai","cloudfront","azureedge","trafficmanager","windowsupdate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode/inspect the long DNS label — base16/base32-looking content strongly indicates file exfil; confirm the source host runs the vulnerable FHIR/Java service and correlate to a recent inbound XML POST. 2) Contain: sinkhole the parent domain at the resolver, isolate the host if the label decodes to recognizable file content, and rotate secrets the service account could read. 3) Hunt: enumerate all distinct external domains the java process queried in the last 7 days, and check the network-egress UC for the matching attacker-DTD fetch that seeded the parameter entity.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
    | where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteUrl
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isnotempty(DnsQuery)
| where DnsQuery !endswith "in-addr.arpa" and DnsQuery !endswith ".arpa"
| extend LeftLabel = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[0])
| where strlen(LeftLabel) >= 30   // 30+ char leftmost label = data smuggled into a DNS subdomain by XXE parameter-entity OOB
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, LeftLabelLen = strlen(LeftLabel)
| order by LeftLabelLen desc

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually exposes a FHIR service that routes untrusted XML through XsltUtilities.saxonTransform (IG-publisher, validator, conversion utilities are the documented consumers) versus the library merely being on disk. 2) Contain: prioritize internet-facing FHIR servers for upgrade to org.hl7.fhir.utilities 6.9.10; where patching lags, place a WAF rule blocking XML with DOCTYPE/ENTITY on FHIR endpoints (see UC 1). 3) Hunt: for each exposed vulnerable host, run the inbound-payload, SSRF-egress, and DNS-callback UCs over the last 30 days to check for prior exploitation.

Unauthenticated file upload to Langflow deprecated /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} endpoint (CVE-2026-55450) AIExploitation High
Hunts POST requests to Langflow's deprecated /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} endpoint that carry no Authorization/API-key header — the exact unauthenticated exploitation shape of CVE-2026-55450 (space-exhaustion DoS + cache-path info leak). Article-specific because it keys on the concrete vulnerable route, the arbitrary-UUID path segment, and the missing-auth condition, not generic upload traffic. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable route /api/v1/upload/{uuid} plus HTTP POST and an empty Authorization header — the precise unauthenticated exploitation condition described in the advisory and closed by PR #12831's get_flow dependency. Cross-checked against the GitLab advisory mirror and the sibling upload-DoS CVE-2026-55446 on the same endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55450/ • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12831 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55446/
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal automation still calling the deprecated upload endpoint but with a valid session cookie stripped by the proxy before logging (auth header not visible)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) fingerprinting the endpoint
  • Load/performance test harnesses exercising the upload API
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors POSTing probe files to the API
  • Pre-1.9.1 workflows where auth was legitimately not enforced yet
Suppression filter
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","nuclei","zgrab","masscan") and SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0/8")  // drop known-scanner UAs and internal test ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SrcIpAddr and confirm it is external/untrusted; check whether HttpStatusCode is 201 (successful save pre-patch) vs 404/413 (patched host rejecting). Inspect TotalBytes for oversized uploads indicating disk-exhaustion intent. 2) Contain: if external and unauthenticated 201s are seen, block the source IP at the WAF/proxy, and confirm the Langflow instance is >=1.9.1; if not, restrict the endpoint or take the instance off the public internet. 3) Hunt: on the Langflow host, review free disk space and the langflow cache directory for a flood of sha256-named files (UC2); search same SrcIpAddr for other unauth Langflow endpoints (build_public_tmp RCE, shareable-playground file read).
// Langflow reverse-proxy / WAF traffic normalised to ASIM ImWebSession
let Lookback = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/upload/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}"
// unauthenticated = no bearer / api-key header presented
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| summarize UploadReqs = count(), TotalBytes = sum(HttpRequestBodyBytes), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10), Urls = make_set(Url, 5) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where UploadReqs >= 3   // 3+ unauth uploads from one source = exploitation, not a one-off scanner probe
| sort by TotalBytes desc
title: Langflow Unauthenticated Upload Endpoint Access (CVE-2026-55450)

status: experimental
description: Detects POST requests to Langflow's deprecated /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} endpoint, the vulnerable route in CVE-2026-55450 that allowed unauthenticated file upload leading to disk-exhaustion DoS and cache-path disclosure.

  condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: high

Langflow cache flooded with SHA256-named upload files — disk-exhaustion DoS (CVE-2026-55450) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a burst of file-creation events under a Langflow cache directory where filenames are 64-hex SHA256 hashes — the on-disk footprint of mass unauthenticated uploads exploiting CVE-2026-55450 to exhaust server disk space. Article-specific because it matches the exact save path pattern (langflow cache + sha256.<ext>) shown in the advisory's PoC response. Rationale: Matches the concrete on-disk artifact from the advisory's PoC response — files saved under a langflow cache folder named with a 64-char SHA256 (e.g. 9d63...5c8.txt) — and thresholds on burst volume, which is the space-exhaustion DoS behaviour rather than a single legitimate upload. Corroborated via the GitLab advisory mirror and sibling CVE-2026-55446. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55450/ • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12831 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55446/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authenticated users bulk-uploading documents for RAG ingestion into flows
  • Scheduled batch ingestion jobs writing many files into a flow's cache
  • Langflow component/artifact caching during heavy flow builds
  • Admin restore of the cache directory from backup (mass file creation)
  • Automated test suites that upload many fixtures against the instance
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("backup-svc","langflow-admin"))  // exclude known bulk-ingest/backup service accounts on the Langflow host
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the host's free disk space and whether the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName = python/uvicorn) is the Langflow service; correlate the burst window with UC1 unauthenticated POSTs from the same timeframe. 2) Contain: if uploads are unauthenticated/external, block the source at the proxy, and if disk pressure is critical, purge attacker-written cache files and confirm the instance is >=1.9.1 (which enforces max_file_size_upload / HTTP 413). 3) Hunt: enumerate all flow-id subfolders under the langflow cache for anomalous growth; pivot on the source IP for other Langflow endpoint abuse; verify no follow-on exploitation used the leaked absolute cache path.
// Server hosting Langflow (Windows or Defender-for-Endpoint on Linux)
let Lookback = 2h;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has "langflow"                       // 'has' is case-insensitive -> Caches/.cache/Cache
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{64}\."   // sha256-named upload artifact per PoC response
| summarize FileCount = count(), TotalBytes = sum(FileSize), DistinctFlowFolders = dcount(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleFolder = any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50   // >50 hash-named cache files in 10m from one process = flood
| sort by TotalBytes desc
let Lookback = 2h;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has "langflow"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{64}\."
| summarize FileCount = count(), TotalBytes = sum(TargetFileSize), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SamplePath = any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50
| sort by TotalBytes desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*langflow* OR *Langflow* OR *LANGFLOW*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/langflow/i
| TargetFileName=/[0-9a-f]{64}\.[a-z0-9]+$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| count > 50

Sapphire Sleet easy-day-js RAT C2 beacon to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two confirmed Hostwinds C2 hosts used by the Mastra/easy-day-js supply-chain RAT: 23.254.164.92:8000 (first-stage dropper download) and 23.254.164.123:443 (second-stage RAT callback). Connections from node.exe to these IPs during or shortly after an npm install are near-certain compromise. Rationale: Anchored on the two C2 IPs (23.254.164.92:8000, 23.254.164.123:443) confirmed by Microsoft, StepSecurity and JFrog as the dropper-download and RAT-callback hosts; pure IOC match so alerting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel detonation sandbox or malware-analysis VM deliberately running the sample
  • Security researcher reproducing the supply-chain attack in a lab
  • Honeypot/canary host intentionally executing the malicious package
  • Shared Hostwinds VPS range later re-allocated to a benign tenant (validate IP is still flagged before alerting long-term)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which local process opened the socket (expect node.exe) and whether an `npm install`/`npm ci` ran on the host in the prior 5 minutes; pull the parent npm command line and the user context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node.exe RAT process tree, and block 23.254.164.92 + 23.254.164.123 at the egress proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: enumerate node_modules for easy-day-js@1.11.22 and any @mastra package at the malicious versions; rotate any developer npm tokens, browser-stored crypto-wallet seeds and session cookies on the host (RAT inventories 166 wallet extensions).

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js postinstall dropper spawning node.exe with C2 IP passed as argument AIInstallation High
Hunts the dropper's second-stage launch: setup.cjs spawns node.exe against a temp .js file passing the RAT C2 host '23.254.164.123:443' as a command-line argument. The literal C2 IP in a node command line is a near-zero-FP signal of the easy-day-js dropper. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim dropper code `child_process.spawn(process.execPath, [file, '23.254.164.123:443'])` — node.exe carrying the C2 IP as argv is an exact-string IOC, hence alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes

  • Lab reproduction of the attack chain by a researcher
  • Highly unlikely benign coincidence: an internal tool legitimately taking 23.254.164.123 as an argument (validate ownership before suppressing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full process tree — expect npm/npx -> node (setup.cjs) -> node (<temp>\<hex>.js 23.254.164.123:443); note the temp script path and the spawning user. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the detached node.exe RAT, and quarantine the temp .js (it self-deletes setup.cjs, so grab it fast). 3) Hunt: search the same user/host for easy-day-js in node_modules and outbound traffic to 23.254.164.92/.123; review browser wallet-extension and history access by the RAT.

Malicious easy-day-js package installed into node_modules AIDelivery High
Hunts the supply-chain footprint itself: files for the typosquatted easy-day-js package (a malicious dayjs clone) being written into node_modules, including its setup.cjs postinstall dropper. Presence indicates the host pulled the compromised @mastra dependency tree. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete package name `easy-day-js` (the malicious dayjs clone, v1.11.22) named in the article and every corroborating vendor write-up; the path node_modules\easy-day-js is unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-hits-mastra-ai-in-npm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js

Node.js writing a random 24-hex-char .js dropper to the OS temp directory AIInstallation Medium
Behavioural fallback that survives C2-IP rotation: detects node.exe writing a randomly-named JavaScript file (crypto.randomBytes(12) -> 24 lowercase hex chars + .js) into the OS temp directory, which is exactly how the easy-day-js postinstall stages its second-stage payload before spawning it detached. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim dropper line `path.join(os.tmpdir(), crypto.randomBytes(12).toString('hex') + '.js')` — 12 random bytes hex-encode to a 24-char lowercase pattern, a tight behavioural signature independent of the (rotatable) C2 IPs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/over-140-popular-mastra-npm-packages-hit-by-supply-chain-attack • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tools that hash-name temp scripts (some bundlers/test runners like jest/ts-node cache transforms in temp)
  • Electron/node CLI apps writing scratch scripts to temp
  • Local dev tooling generating temp ESM shims
  • AV/EDR sandbox that itself drops node temp scripts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest","ts-node","webpack","vite","\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the temp .js still exists (the dropper self-deletes setup.cjs, often leaving the staged file briefly) and whether the writing node.exe parent is an npm install; capture the file for analysis. 2) Contain: if a detached node.exe spawned from that temp path is beaconing to 23.254.164.123, isolate the host and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate with easy-day-js in node_modules and any 23.254.164.92/.123 connections; widen to other dev hosts that ran npm install in the same window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\Temp\"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Temp\"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

rclone process spawning child command (CVE-2026-49980 inline-remote RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the command-execution payload of CVE-2026-49980 / CVE-2026-41179: rclone shells out a local command during backend initialization when an unauthenticated request supplies an inline remote with a command-bearing backend option (webdav bearer_token_command or sftp ssh=). rclone is not a normal parent of arbitrary shells/binaries, so any non-rclone child of rclone on an rcd/--rc-serve host is high-fidelity. Rationale: Pivots on rclone-as-parent of any non-rclone, non-helper child — the observable end of the CVE-2026-49980 chain where a single unauthenticated GET/HEAD forces backend init to exec a local command. The PoC (bearer_token_command='/usr/bin/touch ...') confirms rclone forks an arbitrary attacker-named binary, so child name is variable but the parent is fixed; ssh/fusermount excluded as legitimate rclone backend/mount helpers. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-41179 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rclone/rclone/CVE-2026-49980/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • rclone configured with an sftp backend that uses an external ssh binary (ssh= option) for a legitimate remote — spawns ssh
  • rclone mount/serve teardown invoking fusermount/fusermount3 to unmount a FUSE volume
  • Admin-run rclone with a backend hook or wrapper script that legitimately shells out
  • Backup automation where rclone is wrapped to call a post-transfer notify command
  • Container entrypoints where rclone is PID 1 and legitimately execs a sidecar
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("ssh","ssh.exe","fusermount","fusermount3","scp","scp.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the rclone InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the rclone instance is running `rcd`/`--rc-serve` without `--rc-user`/`--rc-pass`/`--rc-htpasswd`, and check whether the child is a shell/recon binary (sh, bash, id, whoami, curl) vs a known backend helper. 2) Contain: isolate the host or kill the rclone process and block inbound to its rc port (default 5572); rotate any credentials readable by the rclone process user. 3) Hunt: search the same host's web/proxy logs for inbound requests containing `bearer_token_command`/`vendor=other`, enumerate other internet-reachable rclone rc listeners, and confirm patched to >=1.74.3.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rclone","rclone.exe")
| where FileName !in~ ("rclone","rclone.exe","ssh","ssh.exe","fusermount","fusermount3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "rclone"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "rclone" or ActingProcessName endswith "rclone.exe"
| where not(TargetProcessName endswith "rclone" or TargetProcessName endswith "rclone.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "ssh" or TargetProcessName endswith "ssh.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "fusermount" or TargetProcessName endswith "fusermount3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inline-remote connection-string injection in request to rclone rc (bearer_token_command) AIDelivery High
Hunts the actual CVE-2026-49980 exploit request: an unauthenticated GET/HEAD to the rclone rc listener whose URL embeds an inline remote with a command-executing backend option. The strings bearer_token_command, vendor=other and sftp,ssh= inside an HTTP request URI are not produced by normal rclone clients and are the exploit signature. Rationale: The string bearer_token_command (webdav backend) and sftp,ssh= are the exact inline backend options the GHSA/Endor PoC plants to gain code execution (fs=:webdav,...,bearer_token_command='...':). Seeing them in a request URI to the rc port (default 5572) is an unambiguous exploit attempt with essentially no benign source. Defender AH has no web-request table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-41179 • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Nuclei) firing a CVE-2026-49980 template against the rc listener
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement validating the patch
  • WAF or reverse proxy logging a blocked exploit attempt (still worth surfacing)
  • Security researchers replaying the public PoC in a lab that ships logs to prod SIEM
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei", "Nessus", "Qualys", "zgrab") and SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8 scanner range — replace with your authorized scanner IPs")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract SourceIP and full RequestURL — decode the inline remote to read the command in bearer_token_command/ssh=, and determine if the rc target actually responded 200/206 (HEAD/GET serving) vs blocked. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, take the rc listener off the network or enable `--rc-user`/`--rc-pass`, and treat the host as compromised if the request reached an unpatched (<1.74.3) rclone. 3) Hunt: pivot to that host's process telemetry for an rclone-parented child (UC1) within seconds of the request, and sweep all proxy logs for the same SourceIP hitting other internal hosts on 5572.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("bearer_token_command", "vendor=other", "sftp,ssh=", ":webdav,", ":sftp,", ":local,")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed unauthenticated rclone rc deployment (rcd --rc-serve without auth) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-49980 preconditions in your own estate: rclone launched with the rc enabled (rcd/--rc-serve) and bound to a non-localhost address (--rc-addr) but missing --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd. These are the exact unauthenticated, network-reachable, file-serving deployments the advisory says are exploitable. Rationale: Encodes the advisory's stated preconditions verbatim (--rc-serve + rc reachable via --rc-addr + no --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd), surfacing exploitable hosts before an attacker finds them. Localhost binds are filtered out because default rclone only serves the rc to localhost and is not remotely reachable. Cross-checked against: • https://rclone.org/commands/rclone_rcd/ • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rclone/rclone/CVE-2026-49980/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • rclone bound to a trusted internal-only interface protected by an external firewall/security group (reachable in cmdline but not from untrusted networks)
  • Deployments that supply rc credentials via the config file or RCLONE_RC_USER/RCLONE_RC_PASS env vars instead of CLI flags (auth present but invisible to this query)
  • Short-lived rclone rcd test runs by an admin during troubleshooting
  • Hosts already patched to >=1.74.3 where the deployment is no longer exploitable
  • --rc-addr bound to a unix socket path rather than a TCP IP (not network-exposed)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr 127.0.0.1" or ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr localhost" or ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr unix://")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the --rc-addr value resolves to a non-loopback, internet- or untrusted-network-reachable interface and that auth is genuinely absent (check config file and RCLONE_RC_* env vars before declaring exposed). 2) Contain: add --rc-user/--rc-pass or --rc-htpasswd, or drop --rc-serve if file serving is not needed, and restrict the listener with host firewall rules; schedule upgrade to >=1.74.3. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against UC1 (rclone-parented child) and UC2 (bearer_token_command in proxy logs) to determine whether any exposed instance was already exploited.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("rclone","rclone.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-serve" or ProcessCommandLine has "rcd"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--rc-user","--rc-pass","--rc-htpasswd"))
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr 127.0.0.1" or ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr localhost")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessName endswith "rclone" or TargetProcessName endswith "rclone.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--rc-serve","rcd")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr"
| where not(TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--rc-user","--rc-pass","--rc-htpasswd"))
| where not(TargetProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr 127.0.0.1" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr localhost")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] LiteLLM recon probes (/health,/version,/docs) followed by admin-route access from same source · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] LiteLLM auth bypass: malformed Host header on admin/management routes (CVE-2026-49468) · [LLM] LiteLLM unauthenticated successful write to management endpoint (CVE-2026-49468) · [LLM] LiteLLM auth bypass: 401-then-200 to same admin route with identical Host header
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] LiteLLM post-bypass rapid state-changing admin writes (key/user/team mutation burst)
LiteLLM auth bypass: malformed Host header on admin/management routes (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation High
Hunts the root cause of CVE-2026-49468 — a crafted Host header used to make get_request_route() evaluate a different route than FastAPI dispatched. A legitimate Host is only hostname[:port]; any Host carrying a slash, '@', whitespace or '..' reaching a LiteLLM management endpoint (/key,/user,/team,...) is the injection signature. Rationale: Uses the article's exact root-cause (Host-header-driven route evaluation in get_request_route) and the confirmed LiteLLM management route prefixes (/key,/user,/team,...). A Host value containing path/@/whitespace chars is never legitimate, making this high-fidelity. defender_kql/falcon/cloudwatch/datadog empty: Defender XDR, Falcon FDR and the listed Datadog/CloudTrail sources do not ingest reverse-proxy HTTP access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/litellm/CVE-2026-49468/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/ • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1190 T1036
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Burp, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei, Nessus) deliberately fuzzing the Host header during an authorised pentest
  • A misconfigured upstream proxy that forwards a comma-joined X-Forwarded-Host chain into the Host field
  • Service-mesh / sidecar that rewrites Host to include a path-style virtual-host
  • IPv6 literal Host values bracketed oddly by a buggy client (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Nuclei","ZAP","sqlmap","masscan") and SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP/Host pair; confirm the Host value is malformed (contains /,@,space,..) and which management endpoint it targeted, and whether the response was 2xx (successful bypass) vs 401/403. 2) Contain: if any 2xx returned, treat as compromise — rotate the LiteLLM master key and all virtual keys, and block the source IP at the upstream WAF/LB; confirm proxy is upgraded to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: review /key, /user, /team write operations from that source for created keys or deleted users; correlate with UC for unauthenticated admin writes and rapid state-change abuse.
ImWebSession

| where Url has_any ("/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/")
| where isnotempty(HttpHostName)
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[\\/@\s]" or HttpHostName contains ".."
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc
